title: DPA executive one-pager: key commitments & examples
content:
Purpose:
This is a short, customer-facing (exec-friendly) one-pager summarizing the key commitments Redwood makes in a standard DPA for inference services, plus two illustrative examples customers often ask about. Aim: reduce time-to-agreement by surfacing the most common negotiation points in plain language and showing concrete clause language we can offer as a starting point.

Notes on tone and use:
- Not a substitute for the full DPA; this is an executive summary for legal and procurement review.
- Keep it short on calls-to-action: accept our standard language, or propose a single redline per section.
- Use with sales/AE when customers ask "what will you actually promise?"

Key commitments (high level)
1) Data controller/processor roles
   - Redwood role: processor for inference queries and ephemeral service logs; customer remains the data controller for customer-submitted content.
   - Example plain language: "Customer is the Controller of Customer Data; Redwood is a Processor processing Customer Data on Customer’s behalf solely to provide the inference service and related support."

2) Purpose limitation and permitted processing
   - We process only for the service, diagnostics, troubleshooting, billing, and required legal compliance. No retraining on customer data by default.
   - Example clause snippet: "Processor shall not use Customer Data to train, improve, or develop models without Customer’s prior written consent. Processor may use aggregated, de-identified telemetry for service improvement provided it cannot be reverse-engineered to re-identify Customer Data."

3) Data retention and deletion
   - Default: short-term retention of request logs and KV cache (configurable). We provide options: ephemeral retention (no logs), 30/90/365-day tiers, or contract-specific retention.
   - Quick example: "Retention: Request payloads and inference outputs will be retained for 30 days by default for debugging and fraud detection; customers may elect a 0-day retention setting at no extra charge for qualifying plans."

4) Subprocessors and notifications
   - We maintain a subprocessor list and notify customers of material changes. For critical subprocessors (hosting, KMS), customers can request a review period or opt-out where reasonable (enterprise deals).
   - Example: "Processor shall notify Customer of additions or material changes to subprocessors 30 days before engaging them. Customer may object within 15 days, and the parties will use good-faith efforts to resolve."

5) Security controls and attestations
   - Commit to industry baseline: encryption in transit and at rest, MFA for admin console, role-based access controls, periodic penetration testing and SOC/ISO evidence on request for enterprise customers.
   - Example language: "Processor will maintain administrative, physical, and technical safeguards consistent with industry standards and will provide SOC 2 Type II or ISO 27001 certification evidence upon Customer’s written request and subject to NDAs."

6) Incident response and notification timelines
   - Notify customers within 72 hours of confirming a security incident affecting Customer Data; provide root cause and remediation plan within agreed SLA windows.
   - Example timeline: "Initial notification: within 72 hours of confirming a Security Incident; Preliminary remediation plan: within 10 business days; Final report: within 30 calendar days (unless law enforcement restricts disclosure)."

7) Audit, forensics, and evidence preservation
   - Provide reasonable cooperation for customer audits or legal requests; for on-prem/private deployments provide evidence artifacts and access modalities defined in the contract.
   - Example: "Processor will preserve logs and relevant artifacts for a commercially reasonable period for forensics if requested by Customer as part of an incident response or lawful process."

8) Data location and cross-border transfer
   - Regional hosting options + standard SCCs/MFAA or equivalent transfer mechanisms; enterprise customers can negotiate strict residency with dedicated deployments.
   - Example short statement: "Processor will store and process Customer Data in the region(s) specified in the Ordering Document. Transfers outside the region will be subject to appropriate transfer safeguards."

9) Liability and indemnity (summary)
   - We propose customary limits tied to fees and carveouts for willful misconduct. We generally do not accept open-ended downstream liability for customer uses of generated outputs.
   - Helpful negotiation play: offer a limited indemnity for IP infringement tied to output where customer followed documented safe-use guidance.

Two concrete customer scenarios (FAQs + starting language)
A) Customer asks: "Will you use our queries to train your models?"
   - Quick answer: Not without your consent.
   - Starting DPA/contract language: "Processor shall not use Customer Data to train, refine, or otherwise improve any machine learning model or generative model without the Customer’s prior written consent. For clarity, aggregated and irreversibly de-identified telemetry may be used for performance monitoring only."

B) Customer asks: "We need guaranteed 0-day retention for PII queries (no logs kept). Is that possible?"
   - Quick answer: Yes for many plans; approach differs by deployment mode. Hosted: ephemeral mode (no request-body retention) with limited audit visibility. Dedicated/private: can be configured and verified by attestation.
   - Suggested clause: "Processor agrees to operate the Service in Ephemeral Mode for Customer Data, configured to avoid persistent storage of request payloads or output. Processor shall not retain Customer Data beyond transient buffers necessary to serve the request. Processor will provide an attestation describing configuration and controls within 15 business days of request."

Practical negotiation guidance for AEs and legal ops
- Offer defaults that minimize back-and-forth: 30-day logs, model-training opt-out, SOC 2 evidence.
- For enterprise: highlight Private/Dedicated deployment options for stronger residency and retention controls.
- Use a single redline approach: ask customers to consolidate asks into one annotated doc and return.
- Price the operational burden: 0-day retention, per-customer tooling, or special subprocess restrictions may require uplift.

Appendix: sample clause bank (pick one)
- Subprocessor notice clause: "Processor will maintain a current list of subprocessors and will give Customer at least thirty (30) days prior written notice of any new subprocessor engagement that will process Customer Data. Customer may reasonably object to such new subprocessor on lawful data protection grounds, and the parties will seek to resolve any dispute in good faith."
- Incident notification clause: "Processor shall notify Customer without undue delay and in any event within seventy-two (72) hours after becoming aware of a Security Incident affecting Customer Data, and shall provide reasonable updates until the matter is resolved."

Open questions / drafts to finalize before go-live with sales:
- Standard retention tiers and pricing uplift schedule for 0/30/90/365-day options.
- Exact SLA windows for interim and final incident reporting (legal prefers 72h initial; engineering requests 96h for complicated incidents).
- Standard attestation template for ephemeral mode and forensics support levels.

Notes to self:
- Coordinate with product/hosting to publish an internal matrix mapping retention tiers to deployment modes (hosted/dedicated/private) and required engineering/ops actions.
- Draft customer-ready annex for ephemeral mode and add to the DPA templates.

Contact for questions: Priya Kapoor (security-and-compliance).

End of one-pager.
